title: Exact pivotal e-variables for infinite hypotheses: a binary construction and what pivotality costs
oneLine: Any score separating the alternatives from the span of the nulls becomes a coin that is fair under every null; betting on it gives exact, pivotal evidence with the best guarantee from the margin alone, while for unbounded evidence pivotality can cost all the power.
abstract: An e-value measures evidence against a hypothesis like the payoff of a fair bet against it; its quality is the expected logarithm under the alternative (e-power). When the null is a whole family of distributions, an e-variable is exact if its expectation is one under every null and pivotal if its whole distribution is the same under every null. Zhang, Ramdas and Wang characterised bounded exact e-variables with uniformly positive e-power for infinite families by a closure condition and conjectured a pivotal version (Conjecture 6.9). This candidate turns any bounded score separating the alternatives from the null span by a margin δ into a coin that is fair under every null and biased under every alternative; betting the fraction δ gives a bounded exact pivotal e-variable with e-power at least I(δ) = [(1+δ)log(1+δ) + (1−δ)log(1−δ)]/2, and no guarantee depending only on δ is larger. This proves the sufficiency direction of the conjecture and gives a transport-free proof of the step of the finite existence theorem that produces exact pivotal p- and e-variables. For unbounded e-variables pivotality can cost all the power: in an example with one alternative an exact e-variable has e-power at least (1/4)log(27/16) ≈ 0.13 while every pivotal one has none. The sentence of Theorem 6.8 about tightness is false; weak compactness in L¹ repairs it, and under it the conjecture holds in both directions. Limits: one observation; no general formula for the best pivotal e-variable; no full characterisation for unbounded pivotal e-variables; the separating score is computable by linear programming only for finite tables. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 3.1 (proof): under domination and common randomisation, margin δ > 0 is equivalent to the existence of a bounded exact pivotal e-variable with uniformly positive e-power; the coin B = 1{U ≤ (1+h)/2} is fair under every null, and E = 1 + δ(2B − 1) has uniform e-power I(δ).
Theorem 3.2 (proof): I(δ) is the best guarantee that depends on δ alone; in a given experiment richer pivotal e-variables can do better (Remark 3.3).
Corollary 3.4 (proof): the "if" direction of Zhang, Ramdas and Wang's Conjecture 6.9 in bounded form, and a transport-free proof of (e) ⇒ (a),(b) in their finite Theorem 6.1.

Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 4.5 (proof): a pivotal statistic has the null law under any alternative in the closed span of the nulls; an experiment with one alternative has an exact e-variable with e-power at least (1/4)log(27/16) ≈ 0.13 while every pivotal e-variable has none.

Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.4 (proof): the tightness sentence of Theorem 6.8 is false even on a compact space; under weak compactness of conv Q in L¹ the conjecture holds in both directions. Section 7: margin 6/31 with binary guarantee 0.0188, best pivotal e-power 0.0392 and exact optimum about 0.0556.

narration:
This is an audio briefing from Evidence Press on a research candidate about exact and pivotal e-values.

Start with what an e-value is. It is a number that measures evidence against a hypothesis, like the payoff of a fair bet against it. If the hypothesis is true, its average is at most one, so large values are unlikely by chance. Its quality is how fast the evidence grows when the hypothesis is false.

Often the hypothesis is not one distribution but a whole family, because of unknown nuisance parameters. Two stronger demands then make sense. An exact e-value averages exactly one under every member of the family. A pivotal e-value has the same distribution under every member, so its behaviour is known even though the true member is not.

Zhang, Ramdas and Wang showed that for finitely many distributions such e-values exist exactly when the alternatives stay away from the span of the nulls, using optimal transport. For infinite families they conjectured a pivotal version.

The new idea fits in one picture. Take any bounded score that averages zero under every null and at least a margin, delta, under every alternative. Flip a coin whose chance of heads rises with the score. It is fair under every null and biased under every alternative. Bet a fraction delta of your stake on heads. The result is exact and pivotal, and its growth is the best that delta alone can guarantee. This proves the sufficient half of the conjecture by a short route. The ingredients are classical; what is new is that they suffice for infinite families.

There are two further findings. When e-values may be unbounded, pivotality can cost everything: there is an example where an exact e-value gains evidence but every pivotal one is powerless. And one sentence of the earlier paper, about tightness, is false; weak compactness is the right condition, and under it the conjecture holds both ways.

Some limits matter. The results concern one observation, there is no general formula for the best pivotal e-value, and the separating score must still be found for each problem.

This is an unrefereed candidate. Its checking is internal AI-assisted review and computation, not peer review. This briefing uses a synthetic voice and is not additional evidence.

decisionObject.description: Know when exactly calibrated, pivotal e-values exist for infinite composite nulls, what growth they can guarantee, and what pivotality costs.
decisionObject.scope: Sufficiency direction of Conjecture 6.9 with the best guarantee in δ; bounded form in both directions; compact case; cost of pivotality for unbounded e-variables; one observation; no general optimal pivotal e-variable.
